title: Compound Interest Explained Simply (With $50 a Month)
description: Compound interest explained simply with $50 a month: why the first years feel slow, what starting eight years earlier is worth, and the catches.

cover.alt: Five stacks of coins growing taller, with a small plant on top of the tallest

keywords: compound interest explained simply how compound interest works compound interest example rule of 72 saving early
takeaways: Compound interest means your growth starts earning growth of its own.
In the example, starting at 22 instead of 30 turns the same $50 a month into about $52,000 more by 60.
The early years look slow. Keep going, avoid high-interest debt, and leave the money alone.
body:
Fifty dollars a month does not sound like a retirement plan. It sounds like a phone bill, or a couple of takeaway pizzas. Yet compound interest is where a small, ordinary amount of money can turn into a surprisingly large one, given enough time. Here is the short version, using two savers. Both put away $50 a month at an assumed 7% a year. One starts at 22, the other at 30. Both stop at 60. The early starter pays in $22,800 of their own money and ends with about $113,025. The later starter pays in $18,000 and ends with about $60,999. Same monthly amount, same assumed growth rate. The only difference is eight years, and in this example those eight years are worth about $52,026. That 7% is an illustration rate, picked to show the maths clearly. It is not a promise, and it is not what a normal savings account pays. The honest warnings come further down. First, the idea itself, because once you see how it works, the big numbers stop looking like magic. ## Compound interest, in plain words Interest is money you are paid for keeping your money somewhere, worked out as a percentage of your balance. With simple interest, you earn that percentage on your original deposit only, year after year, and the interest itself just sits there doing nothing. Compound interest adds one twist. Each time interest is paid, it joins your balance. From then on, you earn interest on your original money plus all the interest already added. Your interest starts earning interest of its own. Investor.gov, the investor education site run by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, defines it in almost exactly those terms: interest paid on the starting amount plus the interest that has built up. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis uses the short version: interest on interest. Nothing is being created out of thin air. Your balance is simply measured against a bigger pile each time, because last period's growth stays in the pile instead of being skimmed off. You will meet compounding in savings accounts, in investments where returns stay invested, and, less happily, in credit card balances. The maths is identical in all three. Only the direction changes. ## Simple interest vs compound interest, side by side Words only go so far, so here is the difference in numbers. Take a single deposit of $1,000, leave it alone, and apply the same assumed 7% a year in two different ways. With simple interest, every year adds the same $70, always worked out on the original $1,000. With compound interest, the 7% applies to the whole balance, which keeps growing. In the compound column, interest is added monthly. | Years left alone | Simple interest | Compound interest | Extra from compounding | |------------------|-----------------|-------------------|------------------------| | 10 | $1,700 | $2,010 | $310 | | 20 | $2,400 | $4,039 | $1,639 | | 30 | $3,100 | $8,117 | $5,017 | After ten years the gap is $310. Noticeable, but hardly life changing. After thirty years the compound balance is more than two and a half times the simple one, and $5,017 of it exists only because interest was allowed to earn interest. Time did the heavy lifting, and it did most of it late. That pattern, slow then fast, runs through every example in this article. ## $50 a month: the slow first years nobody shows you Lump sums are not how most people save, so let us follow this article's plan: $50 a month, an assumed 7% a year, interest added monthly, no withdrawals. Here is how it builds, year by year at first, then at wider milestones. | Year | Money you have put in | Balance | Growth so far | |------|-----------------------|----------|---------------| | 1 | $600 | $620 | $20 | | 2 | $1,200 | $1,284 | $84 | | 3 | $1,800 | $1,997 | $197 | | 4 | $2,400 | $2,760 | $360 | | 5 | $3,000 | $3,580 | $580 | | 10 | $6,000 | $8,654 | $2,654 | | 20 | $12,000 | $26,046 | $14,046 | Read the first line again. After a full year of saving, the growth is under $20. This is where a lot of people decide the whole thing is pointless and stop, and honestly, it is hard to blame them. Even at year five, the balance is only $580 ahead of what was paid in. Look at what happens later, though. By year 10, growth has quietly passed $2,600. Somewhere between years 15 and 20, it catches up with everything you have paid in, then moves ahead of it. By year 20 the account holds $26,046, of which $14,046 is growth, more than the $12,000 that came out of your pocket. Compounding does not pay you evenly. It pays you near the end for patience you showed at the start. ## Starting at 22 vs starting at 30 Two people, the same $50 a month, the same assumed 7%, both stopping at 60. The only difference is when each begins. | Age | Started at 22: balance | Paid in so far | Started at 30: balance | Paid in so far | |-----|------------------------|----------------|------------------------|----------------| | 30 | $6,410 | $4,800 | Not started | $0 | | 40 | $21,536 | $10,800 | $8,654 | $6,000 | | 50 | $51,934 | $16,800 | $26,046 | $12,000 | | 60 | $113,025 | $22,800 | $60,999 | $18,000 | The early starter pays in $4,800 more across a lifetime: eight extra years of $50. They finish with about $52,026 more. Those first eight years of small deposits produce more growth than the thirty years of deposits that follow them, because early money has the longest time to compound. The later starter cannot fix this by saving the same $50 for longer, because the finish line is the same age. To reach roughly the same $113,025 by 60, someone starting at 30 would need to put away about $93 a month instead of $50. Waiting did not just delay the plan. It nearly doubled the monthly price of the same result. If you are reading this at 30, or 35, or 42, do not take the wrong lesson. You have not missed your chance. The best time to start was years ago, and the second best time is this month, because starting at 30 beats starting at 38 by the same maths. Tables like these show the shape of compounding, but your own numbers will differ. To try your own amount, starting age, and rate, the free spreadsheet that goes with this article does the monthly maths for you.

Download the free Compound Growth Calculator (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The compound growth calculator comparing an early and a late starter saving $50 a month](/assets/img/posts/compound-growth-calculator-preview-1180x1075.webp) ## The formula, translated into English You may have seen the formula written as A = P(1 + r/n)^nt. In plain words, it says this. Take your starting amount. Work out the rate for one period: a yearly rate divided by 12 if interest is added monthly. Add 1, then multiply by that figure once for every period the money stays invested. That is all the symbols are doing: adding interest, letting it join the balance, and repeating, hundreds of times. A rough shortcut for doubling is the Rule of 72: divide 72 by your yearly growth rate to get about how many years your money takes to double. At the assumed 7%, that is 72 divided by 7, roughly 10 years. The St. Louis Fed uses this rule in its own explainer, and it is close enough for rough planning. In practice, you never need to run this by hand. Investor.gov offers a free compound interest calculator that does it from a starting amount, a monthly contribution, a number of years, and a rate, and the spreadsheet linked above does the same job on your own computer. ## The honest warnings, before you get excited Three things need saying plainly, because articles about compound interest often skip them. First, the 7% used here is an assumed rate, chosen to make the examples easy to follow. It is not a typical savings account rate, which is usually far lower. Real returns arrive unevenly: some years are strong, some are negative, and nobody can tell you the exact figure in advance. Second, inflation nibbles at the result. Prices tend to rise over time (the St. Louis Fed notes the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of about 2% a year over the longer run). So the $113,025 in the example would not buy what $113,025 buys today. It would still be a large sum, just a little flattered by today's prices. Third, fees and tax reduce what actually compounds. A charge skimmed off each year is money that never earns interest again. None of this makes the idea useless. It means preferring low fees, and treating every projection, including the ones here, as a sketch rather than a contract. ## The same maths works against you Compounding has no loyalty. It grows whatever balance it is pointed at, including money you owe. On a credit card, interest is charged on the unpaid balance, and if part of that balance is unpaid interest from earlier months, you are paying interest on interest in the worst direction. That is why clearing expensive debt usually comes before investing: removing a balance that compounds against you at a high rate beats earning a modest rate somewhere else. If card balances are your problem, start there: [How to Pay Off Credit Card Debt Fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). ## How to get compounding working for you None of this needs a large income. It needs a start, a routine, and time left alone. - Build a small cash cushion first. If every surprise bill forces you to pull money back out, compounding never gets going. A starter emergency fund protects the habit. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/). - Automate a small amount on payday. This article uses $50 a month, but $25 still works; early on, the amount matters less than the years it gets. Set the transfer for payday, so the money leaves before you can spend it. - Money needed within a couple of years usually belongs somewhere steady, like a savings account. Read next: [What Is a High-Yield Savings Account?](/blog/high-yield-savings-account/). Money for goals a decade or more away is where investing comes in. Read next: [How to Start Investing With Little Money](/blog/start-investing-with-little-money/). - Raise the amount when your pay rises. Adding $10 or $20 a month after a pay rise is barely noticeable day to day, but every extra dollar gets the remaining years to compound. - Leave it alone. Every withdrawal removes money that would have kept earning, and a clear goal for the pot makes it easier to protect. Read next: [How to Set Financial Goals You Actually Reach](/blog/set-financial-goals/). That is the whole system. A small amount, started early, repeated monthly, left untouched. Compound interest does the rest, slowly at first, and then much less slowly. ## Frequently asked questions ### What is compound interest in simple words? It is interest earned on your money, plus interest earned on the interest already added. Growth joins your balance, so each new amount of interest is worked out on a slightly bigger pile than the last. ### What is the difference between simple and compound interest? Simple interest is worked out on your original deposit only, so it adds the same amount every year. Compound interest is worked out on your deposit plus all the interest added so far, so what it adds grows each year. On $1,000 at an assumed 7%, that is the difference between $3,100 and about $8,117 after 30 years. ### Is $50 a month really enough to bother with? At this article's assumed 7%, $50 a month from 22 to 60 grows to about $113,025, of which only $22,800 came from your own pocket. The first year looks disappointing, with under $20 of growth. The habit is what you are really building in those early years, because the bigger growth only arrives later. ### Will I actually earn 7% a year? Nobody can promise you that. The 7% here is an assumed figure, used to show how compounding behaves. Savings account rates change over time and are usually much lower, while investment returns move up and down and can be negative in a given year. Run the numbers at a lower rate too, so your plan still makes sense if growth turns out slower. ### Is it too late to start at 30 or 40? No. Starting later means saving more each month, finishing with a smaller pot, or a bit of both, but a later start still beats never starting. Here, a 30 year old saving $50 a month still reaches about $60,999 by 60 at the assumed rate, built from $18,000 of their own money. ### How often does interest compound? It depends on the account. Some add interest monthly, some daily, some once a year. The more often interest is added, the slightly faster the balance grows, because new interest starts earning sooner. When comparing savings accounts, the yearly figure that already includes compounding, APY in the US and AER in the UK, is the fairest one to compare. ## A quick note This article is general education, not financial advice, and every figure in it is an illustration built on an assumed growth rate, not a prediction. Your results will depend on the rates and returns you actually get, plus fees and tax. If you need advice for your own situation, speak to a qualified adviser in your country. ## Sources - [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, Compound Interest Calculator](https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator) - [Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, How Compound Interest Works & How to Estimate It (2018, updated 2025)](https://www.stlouisfed.org/open-vault/2018/september/how-compound-interest-works) - [NatWest, What Is Compound Interest?](https://www.NatWest.com/savings/savings-guides/what-is-compound-interest.html)
